basalt: Dark gray to black, heavy, and fine-grained. You can't see separate crystals. It sometimes has small gas holes.
bituminous-coal: Black, lightweight for its size, and often layered, with shiny and dull bands. It leaves black smudges on your fingers.
conglomerate: Rounded pebbles of different sizes cemented together in a finer, sandy background, like nature's concrete.
gneiss: Light and dark minerals separated into wavy stripes or bands. Grains are coarse enough to see.
granite: Speckled with large, interlocking crystals: glassy gray quartz, pink or white feldspar, and black specks of mica.
limestone-chemical: Usually light gray to tan, fine-grained, with no big pieces. It fizzes with weak acid.
limestone-fossil: Packed with shells, shell pieces, or other fossils cemented together. It fizzes with weak acid.
marble: Sugary, sparkly crystals, often white or streaked with color. Softer than glass, and it fizzes with acid.
obsidian: Shiny black volcanic glass with smooth, curved, shell-like (conchoidal) breaks and sharp edges.
phyllite: Thin layers with a silky, satiny shine, like shiny slate. The layers are often wavy.
pumice: Very light-colored and light-weight, full of tiny holes like a sponge. It can float on water.
quartzite: Very hard, with a glassy, sugary look. It breaks through the grains, not around them, and doesn't fizz in acid.
sandstone: Gritty like sandpaper, with sand-sized grains you can see or feel. It's often tan, red, or brown.
schist: Sparkly and flaky, with lots of shiny mica flakes lined up in layers. It may have garnet 'dots.'
scoria: Dark red-brown or black, full of holes, but heavier than pumice. It usually sinks.
shale: Fine-grained, gray or black, and splits into thin, flat layers. It feels smooth, like hardened mud.
slate: Dark gray, dull, smooth, and splits into flat, hard sheets. It 'rings' when tapped.
calcite: Often white or clear, breaks into slanted boxes (rhombs), hardness 3, and fizzes in weak acid.
copper: Copper-red metal, often with a green or brown tarnish, in twisted, branching shapes. It's malleable.
corundum: Very hard (9), often in barrel-shaped, six-sided crystals. It can be gray, brown, red (ruby), or blue (sapphire).
feldspar: Pink to salmon-colored and blocky, with flat, shiny cleavage faces that meet at nearly right angles.
fluorite: Glassy cubes or octahedrons, often purple or green, sometimes banded. Hardness 4.
galena: Heavy, shiny, lead-gray metal that forms or breaks into cubes. It leaves a gray streak.
gold: Bright golden-yellow metal, very heavy, and soft. It never tarnishes and leaves a gold-yellow streak.
graphite: Soft, black to steel-gray, and greasy-feeling. It leaves a mark on paper, like pencil lead.
gypsum: Soft (you can scratch it with a fingernail), white to clear, sometimes in long blades (selenite) or fibers.
halite: Clear to white cubes, often with stair-step faces. It tastes salty and dissolves in water.
hematite: Silver-gray and metallic, or dull reddish-brown. Its streak is always reddish-brown.
mica: Peels into thin, flexible, shiny sheets, like pages of a book. It can be clear (muscovite) or black (biotite).
olivine: Glassy, olive-green grains or crystals, often in clumps. It's the gem peridot.
pyrite: Brassy, pale gold metallic cubes with striped faces. It leaves a greenish-black streak.
quartz: Glassy, six-sided crystals with pointed tips. Very hard (7), and it breaks with curved fractures.
talc: Very soft (1), greasy or soapy to touch, and usually white, pale green, or gray.
arachnida: Eight legs, two body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen), and no antennae. Spiders, ticks, mites, scorpions.
chilopoda: Long, flat body with ONE pair of legs on each segment, long antennae, and fast movement. Centipedes.
crustacea: Two pairs of antennae, many legs, and a hard, segmented shell. Pill bugs, sow bugs, crayfish, crabs.
diplopoda: Long, round body with TWO pairs of legs on most segments. Slow, and often curls into a spiral. Millipedes.
archaeognatha: Wingless, humped back, big eyes that touch on top, and three tail filaments, the middle one longest. Jumping bristletails.
blattodea: Flat, oval body, long antennae, and a head tucked under a shield. Cockroaches. Termites are pale, soft, and ant-like.
coleoptera: Hard front wings (elytra) that meet in a straight line down the back, and chewing mouthparts. Beetles.
dermaptera: Long, flat, brown body with pincers (cerci) at the tail and short front wings. Earwigs.
diptera: Only ONE pair of wings, big eyes, and tiny knob-like halteres. Flies, mosquitoes, gnats.
ephemeroptera: Delicate triangle-shaped wings held straight up, and 2 or 3 long thread-like tails. Mayflies.
hemiptera: A straw-like beak for sucking. Many have front wings that are half hard and half clear, forming an X. Stink bugs, cicadas, aphids.
hymenoptera: Two pairs of clear wings and often a narrow 'wasp waist.' Ants, bees, wasps.
lepidoptera: Wings covered with colorful scales and a coiled drinking tube (proboscis). Butterflies and moths.
neuroptera: Four clear wings with a lacy net of veins, held like a roof over the body. Lacewings, antlions.
odonata: Long, thin abdomen, huge eyes, and four long, veined wings. Dragonflies and damselflies.
orthoptera: Big jumping back legs and long, straight wings. Grasshoppers, crickets, katydids.
phasmatodea: Long, thin body and legs that look just like twigs or leaves. Stick insects.
psocodea: Tiny, soft insects with big heads. Barklice live on bark; lice are flat and wingless parasites.
siphonaptera: Tiny, wingless, and flattened side to side, with powerful jumping legs. Fleas.
trichoptera: Moth-like, but with hairy wings held like a tent and very long antennae. Larvae build cases in streams. Caddisflies.
zygentoma: Wingless, flat, silvery, carrot-shaped body with three tail filaments. Silverfish.
american-beech: Smooth, light-gray bark (even on big trees), toothed oval leaves with straight veins, and spiky husks around beechnuts.
black-gum: Shiny, oval leaves with smooth edges that turn bright scarlet in fall, blocky bark, and small blue-black berries.
callery-pear: Clouds of white five-petaled flowers in early spring, shiny round leaves with wavy edges, and tiny brown fruits.
crepe-myrtle: Smooth, peeling, mottled bark, and big clusters of crinkly pink, purple, red, or white flowers in summer.
eastern-white-pine: Soft, thin blue-green needles in bundles of 5, and long, narrow, curved cones.
hickory: Compound leaves with 5 to 9 leaflets, and round nuts in thick husks that split into 4 parts.
loblolly-pine: Long needles (6 to 9 inches) in bundles of 3, and prickly cones about 3 to 5 inches long.
longleaf-pine: Very long needles (up to 18 inches) in bundles of 3, big cones (6 to 10 inches), and young trees that look like grass clumps.
magnolia: Big, thick, glossy evergreen leaves, often rusty underneath, large white flowers, and cone-like fruits with red seeds.
oak: Acorns! Leaves often have lobes (rounded or pointed) and grow in clusters at the twig tips.
red-maple: Leaves with 3 to 5 pointed, toothed lobes growing in opposite pairs, red twigs and flowers, and winged 'helicopter' seeds.
river-birch: Shaggy, peeling, papery bark in pinkish-tan and cinnamon curls, and diamond-shaped, double-toothed leaves.
shortleaf-pine: Short needles (3 to 5 inches) in bundles of 2 or 3, and small cones (about 2 inches).
sweetgum: Star-shaped leaves with five points and spiky, ball-shaped 'gumball' seed pods.
english-ivy: Evergreen vine with dark, glossy, 3- to 5-lobed leaves, climbing trees and walls with little rootlets.
carolina-lily: Nodding orange to red flowers with spots, petals that curve back, and leaves in whorls around the stem.
poison-ivy: Leaves of three! The middle leaflet has a longer stalk. It can be a vine with hairy rootlets or a small shrub. Don't touch!
kudzu: A giant vine with three big leaflets, hairy stems, and purple flower clusters, blanketing trees and poles.
scuppernong: A muscadine grape vine with round, toothed leaves and round, thick-skinned bronze-green grapes.
venus-flytrap: Small rosette of leaves ending in hinged, red-lined traps with stiff 'teeth' along the edges.
american-alligator: Huge, dark, armored reptile with a broad, rounded U-shaped snout. Found in eastern NC waters.
green-anole: Small, slender lizard that is bright green or brown, with a pointed snout. Males show a pink throat fan.
five-lined-skink: Shiny, smooth lizard with five light stripes down its back. Young ones have a bright blue tail.
eastern-glass-lizard: Looks like a legless snake, but has eyelids, ear openings, and a groove along its side.
eastern-fence-lizard: Gray-brown with rough, spiny scales and wavy dark bands. Males have blue belly patches.
copperhead: Tan to pinkish body with dark hourglass-shaped (Hershey's Kiss) bands and a coppery head. Venomous!
cottonmouth: Thick, dark body, a wide head with a dark stripe through the eye, and a white mouth lining. Venomous!
eastern-diamondback: Large, heavy snake with dark diamonds outlined in cream, and a rattle on its tail. Venomous!
black-rat-snake: Long, shiny black snake, often with faint patterns and a white chin and throat. Great climber.
dekays-brownsnake: Small, brown snake with two rows of dark spots down its back.
eastern-hognose: Thick body, upturned pointy snout, and blotchy pattern. It may flatten its neck like a cobra.
eastern-kingsnake: Shiny black with narrow white or yellow chain-like bands.
banded-water-snake: Thick-bodied water snake with dark crossbands on a lighter body, often seen near water.
eastern-garter-snake: Three light stripes running down the body, often with a checkered pattern between them.
snapping-turtle: Big head, hooked beak, long tail with a saw-toothed ridge, and a small bottom shell.
painted-turtle: Smooth, dark shell with red and yellow markings on the edges, and yellow stripes on the head.
spotted-turtle: Small, black shell sprinkled with bright yellow polka dots.
eastern-box-turtle: High, domed shell with yellow-orange patterns. The bottom shell has a hinge so it can close up. NC state reptile!
yellow-bellied-slider: A yellow patch or stripe behind each eye and a yellow belly. Often basks on logs.
american-toad: Brown and bumpy, with dry, warty skin and big bumps (glands) behind the eyes.
pine-barrens-treefrog: Bright green with a white-edged lavender or purple stripe along each side. NC state frog!
bullfrog: Very large, green to olive frog with a big round eardrum and no ridges down its back.
southern-leopard-frog: Slim, green or brown frog with dark round spots, a pointed snout, and light ridges down its back.
marbled-salamander: Stout, black salamander with bold silvery-white or gray bands. NC state salamander!
red-backed-salamander: Small, skinny salamander, usually with a red-orange stripe down its back (some are all gray).
white-spotted-slimy-salamander: Shiny black salamander sprinkled with small white or silver spots. Very sticky slime.
